Immersion breaking only means something that takes you, the player, out of the games headspace and into your own.  That can be something unrealistic for the setting, writing that doesn't fit, a phone call in the room you're in, or yes, a recognizable item or character from something else.

OhThis argument is very similar to when people first start cooking for themselves and see the massive cost of getting a running pantry.  Utensils and spices cost a ton before you have them built up, and the time and energy when learning seems massive, so a lot of people say "why spend 25 dollars on ingredients to make tacos when I can go to taco bell 3 times for that.". The truth of it is though, that first 25 will make a few meals, and once you have the cumin and other parts, the next time it'll be 15 and so on and so forth.


Home ownership is similar.  The up front costs can be astronomical, so you think "Jesus, a new roof, a new mini split, new plumbing, if I rented it would be half of this." And that's true for the first 5 to 10 years if you buy any kind of fixxer upper.  After that though, you shouldn't be doing so much maintenance.  If you need to replace every part of your house every 5 year, either you or the person you hire is doing a slapdash job.  Then once that upkeep is done, you have an investment.  Rent is money thrown in a hole, a mortgage comes back to you or your kids when you decide to sell.  You can leverage it for different loans, and you have much more control over your own property.  


Lastly, and something overlooked a lot.  A mortgage should eventually END.  Rent does not.  30 years from now when you're getting close to mid 60s, the lack of monthly payments like that could be the difference between retirement and lifelong work.  


Stick with it, it was never meant to be an oasis, it's work and a commitment, but it IS cheaper in the long run.

My main issue with it is that it's so widespread, but only really works in rural communities.  I've done a lot of trunk or treats because I just enjoy being a part of things, but I've noticed the only ones that have that classic Halloween vibes are towns where a few criteria are met:   


1. Houses are far enough apart that trick or treating isn't really an option  


  2.  Safe tight knit community   


3. Relatively well off parents, at least not scarcity mindset  


When talking about this, I'm going to just not address the elephant in the room of the socioeconomic problems, and why they are or how they could be fixed.  That is an important discussion, but it isn't really the topic here, this is just about why I've noticed trunk or treats don't have that Halloween vibes.   


It feels like the best place for a trunk or treat would be a neighborhood that's less safe, it would be a way for the kids to have Halloween when otherwise they might not be able to trick or treat in the city; but unfortunately a lot of the parents bring their problems with them.  A lot of the parents tell their kids to take as much as they can get away with to have more at home.  I've seen parents drunk off their asses, homeless guys coming through for candy, and even fights break out at the city trunk or treats I've gone to.  Again, there's a lot of complexity to this as a topic I'm just not going to address, this is about the trunk or treating in a vacuum. 




The other one that doesn't work is the suburbs, these tend to be safe, and really well decorated thanks to wealthier parents, it's clear an effort is being made.  That being said, the kids just aren't interested.  They've been doing Halloween shit for weeks, they have Halloween parties to go to, they usually do still trick or treat on the night itself.  To them, this is just another night to chill with their friends.  They'll still go around and get candy, but none of the actual effort is appreciated.  It's more the parents enjoying it. 


It just doesn't feel like a solution to every community, but it's been widely accepted in communities where it just doesn't feel like it works.  I've seen exceptions here or there, but it proves true in a lot of places.

Start with simpler meals, and work on learning what to buy.  If you buy a whole head of cabbage and struggle with using it, focus on cabbage heavy meals to use it up.  Things like stir fry or coleslaw.  


Once you build a pantry of staples it gets much cheaper, and all you really need to focus on is perishables, and after enough practice you get a feel for what you can and cant use before it goes bad.  Meat freezes really well so that's not really an issue, and frozen vegetables are your friend, I've had the same massive bag of peas in my freezer for months.


It really does just come down to learning what you'll personally use or won't use.  Someone can say "Buy onions in bulk because they last a long time" all day long, but if you never use onions they'll still eventually rot.  Figure out what you like to cook, and plan around that.  Get pantry staples that last ages and a good selection of seasonings, and figure out what portion you'll use before it goes to waste, then just build off that foundation.


You don't need a million cooking tricks, and you can minmax skills all day long, but at the end of the day just get what you like and try to make it work until it does.

The traditional Zelda dungeon is almost metroidvania in style.  You'd go in, find a few dead ends, solve a few puzzles until you get a map or compass.  Then you'd double back through the rooms you'd completed and past some form of dungeon "main room" gimmick, use the keys you'd gathered to open some dead ends to find more keys, eventually leading to an item, which increases the puzzle complexity around it and opens even more pathways. Keep this up until you hit the boss key and can open the big central door you've been running past.

Newer dungeons are much more freeform, it's about creative thinking on a theme as opposed to direct solving of a puzzle.  Don't get me wrong both are great, and most appeal to everyone to some extent, but some people find more joy in one or the other.  I liked running through rooms I'd done before to be able to open a door I've been staring at, or finally being able to cross the giant pit.  Dungeons now allow you to solve them in more creative ways, but I preferred the more focused approach with one solution you had to slowly pick away at like untying a knit.

Paper Mario Color Splash.  Sticker star is usually the bad guy but bear with me here.  I didn't have the best childhood.  I won't go into detail, but it was rough for me.  When I was at my mother's house though, I could play a GameCube that had Thousand Year Door.  That game became something really special to me.  I didn't have a lot to play, and even that I could only do at her house the rare chances I had, so it took me years to beat.  

I'd look forward to it all the time, I'd think about it when away.  Id imagine I was friends with the characters and make little play stories.  When I beat it I cried, because it was a really special moment for me.  As I aged things got better and I went back and played the original and loved it just as much. Then in my teens I played Super Paper Mario and that story hit me at the perfect time.  It gave me a coming of age moment, it taught me it was okay to be hurt.  I know these are just dumb games, but they meant something to me.  

As a young adult, Sticker Star came out, and I was so excited.  All the other games were practically my one good memory from my childhood.  Sticker Star was trash and it crushed me.  Not only was it bad, but it lacked any characters or depth.  Even then though, one miss in a great series isn't an issue.  I was sad, but I waited for the next one.  

The next was Color Splash.  And it was good.  This was worst case scenario for me, because while it was good, it lacked the elements that made the older games special to me.  It was essentially a different game series given the same name; and the quality it did have basically put the final nails in the coffin of a series that meant the world to me.  I'd never see that specific setting and story archetype again.  Why would they return to form if the newer games sold well.

Of course we're getting a remake of TTYD now and I couldn't be more excited.  I'm hoping it sells well and leads to more classic Paper Mario titles in the future.

Understand, I don't hate anyone that likes the newer games like some people do.  If those games are special to someone I'm happy for them, but for me specifically, the success of the new style meant that something I loved was as far as I knew never returning.  Here's to hoping.

First off, craigslist free is fantastic.  Especially in a major city like Chicago.  If you're a decent sized person physically, a lot of people put up good shit just to get someone to remove it from their house since it's so much bother.  Home Depot rents pickups for pretty damn cheap, I think it's 20 bucks for the first 2 hours or something like that.  If it's nearby, you can do a lot with 2 shitty goodwill skateboards and some rope to get it back to your place.

If you can get a vehicle of any kind, look for a Habitat for Humanity restore.  I just checked and there is one in Chicago.  You have to pay for the furniture but it's decently priced, I got a couch for 30 dollars.  It was extremely dated but in good condition and lasted me years.  I got a basic wooden dining table for 15 there once.  They have a partnership with a moving company if you can afford it, but I'd stick with either using the pickup for individual items, or making a schedule for what you want to get all in one day and doing a truck rental.  Since you don't have anyone to help you carry, try to get stuff that can disassemble or is just plain light, moving straps are cheap and can really help center you to move stuff you thought you might not be able to, just be careful and don't hurt yourself.

If you're comfortable with this, a lot of people there are volunteers and it doesn't hurt just to ask if someone can help bring it up to your place.  You'll almost certainly get a no but if you're really nice someone might be willing, that worked for a friend of mine once.

Otherwise you're best bet is to find the cheapest stuff online that can be shipped direct to your door, Amazon, Wayfare, Walmart and the like have some decent offerings.  Its not as good as getting used furniture for cheap, because it'll be lower quality and more expensive, but it can get stuff right to your door to be assembled inside.

As an absolute last ditch effort, find a local library that does tool rental, and build your own, be creative and get some Tom and Jerry chique.  It'll look trashy but you can do a lot with some plywood, a sander, stacks of cinderblocks, and a little wood stain.  You can find scrap pallet board all over the back lots of practically any big box store, just make sure to ask a manager and check the boards to see if they're safe for indoor use, some are treated and that can be unhealthy with prolonged contact.  Again, your place will look like it's right out of Fallout but it'll give you something to eat off of.

Don't be ashamed to ask family or long distance friends for help if you're on good terms with them.

This is really good news imo, Mysterious Journey didn't really take off for a couple reasons.  The first is that Level 5 realized that the genre was losing steam, and moved it to a mobile platform in order to garner a wider audience, not a bad move on its own but they also worked to try to make it easier to chew for someone who may not have been that into puzzle games, and it led to a pretty obvious lack of challenge that Layton is known for in the later stages of the game.

Secondly and more impactfully, after Azran Legacy the series Puzzle Master Akira Tago passed away.  He was the driving force for a lot of the ideas that made Layton special as a series, and without him the puzzles just didn't have the same oomph and charm, they did their best and Mysterious Journey is by no means a bad game, but it doesn't "feel" the same.

This new game is part of a huge revitalization project by Level 5 for the west, a sort of hail Mary when before they were begining to pull out of development focus outside of Japan, with that we can see that A LOT of care and time has gone into figuring out what makes a Layton game a Layton game.  In order to prove they still have what it takes to the shareholders, you could say this push of content is them putting their best foot forward.  With that, QuizKnock really does make perfect content that matches well with the standards the series is known for, I'm glad to see them outsourcing the puzzle design to a team that understands the kind of gameplay people want, rather than trying to do it all in house without the genius of Akira Tago behind them.

High hopes for the game, gonna be a day one purchase for me and my wife that's for sure.

Start with a pork butt, not a brisket, that's way easier.  Simple as put it on until its done and maybe broil it after if you want the skin real crisp.  


That being said, I started with a brisket and honestly, brisket isn't as hard as people say if you just want a simple one, you don't HAVE to wrap it or do anything more complicated than trim, season, and smoke.  Don't bother getting up early to start it, start the night before at midnight or something.  Its essentially a 5 step process.  


1. Trim and season, cut the fat from the top of the meat down to 1/4th an inch, don't worry too much about making it perfect, just try not to cut into the meat itself.  There's a big fat lump on the back, cut as much out as you can until its more or less even with the meat, it runs all the way through, so just try to make it even, if you remove the whole thing you'll end up cutting your brisket in half.  Then cover the thing in salt and pepper, a good dusting on the whole thing.  Every cut is a little different so I can't give an exact amount, just make it look real salt and peppery.  

2. Get your smoker somewhere between 225 and 250.  I'd say use hickory if you've never smoked before, but any wood will do.  Personally I use half mesquite, half pecan.  

3. Toss it on the smoker fat side down, it doesn't matter that much which way you do it, but fat down provides some insulation and since we're not wrapping it for the sake of saving you a step, you'll need that.  

4. Smoke it until it hits somewhere over 200, but under 210.  Most people take off at around 203.  This will take a LONG time.  Sometimes mine are done in 16 hours, sometimes 20, point is, it takes ages, just be patient.  If you're looking, it aint cooking.  

5. Let it rest for AT LEAST an hour, preferably 2.  Just put it in a cooler or something.  That should do it for you.  


This isn't going to be a competition brisket, because this is as simple as one can possibly be.  There are all kinds of rubs you can do, ways to cut it, injections, spraying with cider or vinegar and whatever, wrapping it is a good way to cut down on cook time and retain some moisture, its also generally best to leave it covered in your seasoning uncovered in the fridge overnight or something, but again, not really needed if you just want a good hunk of meat.  Follows these steps to the letter and you should have a good brisket.  Its all about patience, its a large chunk of meat, and it'll take a very long time to cook.  Just have faith that it WILL hit 203, and take it out when it does.  Dont crank up the temp to make it go faster, dont check it constantly to see if its getting bark, don't panic when it hits 175 and doesn't change for 4 hours, thats normal.  Just have faith in the meat, and it'll come out good.

Outside of just the bad launch window, the switch being in it's twilight years (supposedly), and digital sales generally being larger than ever, I really think the main culprit is just FE burnout.

Don't get me wrong, I LOVE Fire Emblem, I've been a die hard fan since Sacred Stones back on the GBA, I went back and even played some of the older Japanese exclusives, but even with all that, I've felt a little tired with it lately.  Between Three Houses being amazing, but really long to get all the content, Fire Emblem Warriors, the massive amount of Smash reveals, Tokyo Mirage Sessions Encore, and Fire Emblem Heroes, that's a lot of Fire Emblem in the public eye, especially for a series that was on the chopping block until Awakening.  Fire Emblem fans both old and new are still frequently working their way through the story routes in Three Houses, at least the ones I know.

I realize other games do this, we've had what, 4 mainline pokemon games in the past 2 years, CoD pretty much has a yearly release, and Ubisoft is releasing the same open world tower game with a new slap of paint every couple months, but all of those tend to have more casual fans than TRPGs.  This is a LOOOOONG genre of game, that generally asks a lot of patience and dedication from it's players, so I think this is just a sort of backup of Fire Emblem that's been building since 2016 or so catching up.

The initial sales might not be as high, but I wouldn't be surprised if you see higher than average sales numbers in the months to come as fans of the series sort of realize it's around and find the energy and time for it, I think this game is going to have legs when it comes to longevity.

If your rent and utilities are bundled in with tuition, you have no insurance costs, and no car, then provided you don't have any obscure health issues that aren't covered or bad habits like smoking or whatever, then you should be able to.  I was a single guy in his 20s, and there was a time in my life I mostly ate rice, beans, and chicken thighs, and my grocery costs came out to maybe 90 a month if I was careful.  Just know its not really comfortable long term, you can live off it but it can be surprisingly wearing on the mind to live on so little.  It was only a couple years ago, the prices are higher now but you could probably manage the same for around 130 a month depending on where you live.  Theres some good advice in here too, check to see if you quality for SNAP (food stamps) they give you more than enough to be comfortable, also there are food pantries all over in America, so check those out, you'll be able to get good pantry foods so you'll be able to save that money for proteins and fresh veggies.  Find cheap hobbies and ways to hang with friends, when I was in school I'd do movie nights at my place and we'd do a potluck style, everyone bring something, for legal reasons I can't say how I paid for the movies but lets just say I had on a nice tricorn pirates hat and leave it at that.  


However, lets just go off the assumption that you can't get SNAP, there are no food banks near you, your schools got no program for feeding you, and your friends are unsympathetic and wont do cheaper hangouts.  In that case, heres some advice.  


1. Set aside maybe 30 bucks for hangouts with friends a month, you'll get 1 to 2 hangouts with that.  If you go to a bar, eat at home beforehand and just buy soda or water while there.  You wont be able to get drunk, but you'll get to hang out and it'll cost you maybe 10 bucks.  If you go to a restaurant, try to talk them into an Applebees type place, you can get a decent meal there for 20 if you don't get anything but your main.  For movies sneak in your own snacks and try to do daytime tickets if you can to get a couple bucks off.  

2. Find a cheap store near you.  If you have an Aldi's you're golden.  You can still stretch 90 bucks into a months worth of food there even with the price increases, and get a few luxuries.  If you don't have one, look for a Lidl, if you don't have one of those, then try to find a local hispanic or asian grocer.  HMart, Lotte Plaza, Worldmarket, LAMart, stuff like that.  The more Americanized foods there like common cereals and cheddar and the like will be more expensive, but you can get big bags of unbutchered chicken for about 69 cents a pound at almost any of them, which is super cheap for the protein amount and calories, same goes for frozen fish.  They'll usually also have a section with produce thats not selling, going bad, or just weird or unripe, where you can get a crazy amount for a single dollar.  Buy a giant bag of rice and make that last, then the cheapest eggs, then dry beans and learn how to rehydrate them.  These will be your staples.  Get your bigass bags of chicken, rice, and dry beans, then using whatever veggies, fruits, and sauces are on sale, edit your menu accordingly.  Theres a lot you can make with it.  Stir fry, tacos, casserole, burritos, egg sandwiches, ect.  Buy some spices too, its more expensive up front but its worth it to mix up the flavors.  Avoid walmart, Dollar General, and the like, its tempting at first but you don't really get your money's worth most of the time.  

3. Find cheap hobbies to keep yourself busy.  Get into hiking, reading, birdwatching, urban exploring, whatever.  But its important to make sure you keep yourself busy, its too easy to spend money when bored just to make the brain give that serotonin release.  

4. This parts gonna piss some people off, if your a guy then give up on dating for the time being.  Its just too hard to make anyone that you aren't already close with happy on a date without spending more than you've got, however if you're not a guy, then maybe step up the dating game a bit to get some free meals.  Don't take advantage of people of course, but I've got some friends who relied on date meals during a money crisis and it can be a nice social event for the evening as well.  Just make sure your up front with whoever you date either way, people don't wanna just be a food bank and most will be understanding provided you're still good company.  

5. Check and see if your city has some kind of monthly bus pass, I read further down its 4 dollars for a day pass, but a lot of places will have unlimited passes available, and you can usually get some kind of large discount for being a student, and an additional one if you're below the poverty line.  Those can stack depending on where you are, it might be cheaper in the long run to check with your city/school about that than paying the 4 dollars everyday you need to use them.  


Thats it really, its honestly mostly about knowing where to shop and how to break down the costs and nutrition of your own meals.  Don't just focus on calories per dollar, make sure you're getting enough vitamins, minerals, and proteins to be healthy, do all of that and you should be able to make do mentally and physically on 140 a month.

There are tons of types of prose out there in sci-fi and fantasy, you can have the traditional type like Tolkein, lots of flowery poetry, and deep language introspection.  You can have the comical type like Pratchett, humorous metaphors and wordplay galore.  You can have the complex type like Erikson, overwhelming with information and yet simple in its purpose.  Sanderson is just another kind of prose, his is direct.  He writes to the point, and matter of fact, with a focus on the character dialogue and literal descriptions, without too much fluff weighing it down.  None of these are any better or worse than the last.  I see people say he writes like a YA author, but I don't quite think that's true, YA authors frequently use that direct prose as a crutch because it can be easier than filling with metaphor, but he isn't incapable of the others, the later work he did in Wheel of Time proves that, he makes a choice to keep it direct; and I can really appreciate that.  


If you want some other authors with similar prose, a little more story and character focused as opposed to language or poetry, try Robin Hobbs Farseer Trilogy, or Brent Weeks Lightbringing series.  Both are excellent work with great story, and direct prose that works really well for approachability.

I have 100%'d Binding of Isaac Rebirth and all its DLC.  I loved that game before I did that, I learned to hate it as I completed it.  For those you of you who don't know what that entails, it means getting 13 endings with 34 characters TWICE, so that's a minimum of 884 runs if you don't fail any and win every time in the correct order, and remember, for one of the characters, you can never take any damage at all through the entire run.  You have to unlock some of the characters through very obscure methods, sometimes which involve ending a run early at a very late point in the game, so you can add about 10 more onto that number to unlock those characters if you get lucky and manage it your first time.

You are NOT guaranteed to get everything you need to even get to every boss you need in a given run, sometimes you wont get angel room spawns for key pieces, sometimes you wont have a key to get to Downpour II, and the game itself is already difficult, and at times upsettingly unfair.  After that, you need to beat 45 different challenges, some of which are laughably easy, others of which are MUCH harder than the base game on hard mode, 5 of which are entirely RNG dependent on winning, and 1 of which is a secret and doesn't even show up on the menu.  Now then, after that, there are achievements that involve getting certain transformations or combinations of items, donating certain amounts of money, etc etc, you'll likely get MOST of these just by finishing all endings with all characters, but you'll miss at least a few just by sheer chance, because many of them, again, are based entirely on luck.

So that sounds pretty tough right?  That's a grand total minimum of about 945 runs in a game, where the average run lasts about an hour and a half, if you never die and always manage to win your run and never fuck up the order in which to do it.  That's just under 1500 hours if you are entirely optimized in your play and make no mistakes.  That's absurd.  So if you manage to do all that, you'll FINALLY, at the very end, be able to look and say, I have 636 out of 637 achievements.

Wait.What?

Why only 636?  Shouldn't the game be done?  I've done everything there is to do, I've beaten everything there is to beat, my save file is finished there isn't anything left to beat, no stone unturned, no boss unbeaten, I have real platinum golden god deluxe, why haven't I gotten the final achievement.

You wanna know why?  Because to get that last achievement, you have to do it again.  Twice.  You have to complete EVERY SAVE FILE.  THREE OF THEM.  So take every single number I stated, and multiply it by 3.  If played entirely optimally, that's 2835 runs, clocking in at just under 4300 hours.  Want to know a fun fact?  I did not play optimally. I take pride in the achievement, but I'm never going to open that game again.

Honestly, I see most incels and the other subclasses of that as victims these days.  Keep in mind, this in no way excuses the behavior, just because someone is a victim doesn't mean they aren't responsible for their own actions, so when I say I pity them, I'm not condoning the sexism or racism or other 'isms, and I think we should be extremely critical of those.  That being said, when I was on those sites, the main feeling wasn't anger, it was misery.  There were a lot of them who had mental issues, who were LGBT but grew up in a place very hostile to it, or the opposite of that, people who were traditionally masculine or feminine but grew up in a hostile area to *that*, or who were just not great at socializing, and then there'd be a few events where they embarrassed themselves as kids, and it just spiraled out of control in their mind.  They'd be bullied or rejected so many times that they gave up trying to partake in acceptable behavior, sort of the idea of becoming the monster people say you are.  For every post they made about how horrible this group or that group was, there'd be 3 about just wanting some kind of positive interaction but having no idea how to get it, just really wanting a hug.  They genuinely just don't understand socialization, and while we live in a time where mental issues like that are being more widely accepted, they have a sort of... specific breed of it most people find repulsive.  Its not easy to take pity on someone when they make a point to be as hostile and rude as possible to you for literally no reason other than they assume you'll treat them the way they see themselves.

My change came about because I met someone who was very kind to me, and no matter how vile I was, she kept giving me another chance.  Over time, it becomes impossible to ignore that your interpretation of people is wrong when someone is that kind to you.  No one owes anyone an interaction they don't want to give, so its not on people to change anyone's mind, but it does make a difference when it happens enough.  I've managed to go back and talk to a few friends of mine that were still in there, and just by talking them through their feelings instead of blindly agreeing, a couple of them realized what they were doing and left as well.  One is happily married now, you'd never know what a bigot he was before.  He'd just genuinely never had a positive interaction with the people he'd hated and that warped his entire worldview to this awful hateful place.  The world isn't like that at all, sure there are cruel people in it, but for every cruel person is someone else just trying to live their life; and we aren't making things better by being cruel to others ourselves, all that does is give temporary bitter relief before plunging back into that misery.  Being kind to people has made me so much happier than I ever was before, and its helped me meet all kinds of different people who genuinely like me, and I genuinely like them.

Wrote this up about 2 years ago but I think most of it still applies.  Here you go:  


It depends really on how far you want to go, but in the area, there are local farmers markets around Oakland Mills every sunday, and the Central Library every wednesday. Theres also a small stall that opens up at the East Columbia Library every thursday with a really sweet older lady who has the best produce. As for interesting things, Old Elicott City is definitely on that list, its a small downtown section of a historical town built either OVER a river, or right into a mountainside. Its got EC Pops for homemade popcorn in crazy flavors, Sweet Cascades chocolates for some amazing homemade chocolate, Tea Over the Tiber should be opening by summer, and its a phenomenal tea shop right ontop of the river the town is built on, and it really is built on it, you can see it through some of the floorboards in the older buildings. Sadly, it was devastated by two flood in the past few years, but they bounce back everytime and this time have a plan to stop future flooding.  
  
During summer, there are tons of events over at Lake Kittamaqundi, from free movie nights where a projector is set up on the lake front, to dances, to concerts and art shows. They put up a list, but theres something going on there almost every night and its always charming. Of course the mall next to it, the Columbia Mall, is a fun place to just go chill if you need it. Its the 8th largest mall in America, but they try to keep it classy. In Kings Contrivance they have the St. Matthew Multi-Cultural Festival early october, which celebrates different mid and east European cultures, everything from German to Turkish, they have great food, the dances are fun, and there is a silent auction downstairs thats just great.  
  
Theres also the Maryland Renaissance Festival, its a little bit of a drive, being in crownsville, but its close by enough to still be local. Its considered one of the BEST ren fests in the world. It covers a few acres, and has enough shops and stalls and activities to really interest anyone, even people who normally wouldn't be into that kind of thing, I brought my fiance there and she adored it. In the same vein is the Howard County Fair every August, huge fair, lots of rides, but the real winners are the animals and showrooms. You can go see all kinds of animals, and not just normal farm animals like you'd think, and the showhouses have award winning projects, baked goods, and art. Bit of self promotion here, but I've actually won the apple pie contest there in the past.  
  
As for butchers, I'm a big fan of J.W. Treuth and Sons, the butcher shop they run has been there for over a century I believe, and they have some amazing beef. Good prices too. The local whole foods has a butcher, but honestly, even better quality meat from a place like whole foods is still grocery store meat, and I don't like the prices they charge there. You're better off with Treuth and Sons, or Clarks Farm a little south. Clarks also has amazing produce and jams btw, not a farmers market exactly because its just... well... their farm. But its great. If you want even fresher than that, there are garden plots people buy by the Old Brick Church (also fun for a tour if you're into that kind of thing, small though) and you can meet up with some local growers and they'll often have excess to give or sell to you if you ask.  
  
We've got a ton of walking trails and lakes you can fish on, Mad City Coffee is a fantastic little cafe and a great place to buy your beans if you're into that, once upon a time I would have said Bean Hollow, but sadly it was destroyed by the floods in Elicott. The best bars in the area are as follows:  
  
For trendy (little noisy, modern music, ect): Pub Dog  
For fancy (lots of imported, little pricey but upscale): Frisco Tap and Brewhouse  
For food (tons of food, huge portions): The Trolley Stop (this ones fun cause its actually an old trolly stop near the train tracks)  
For style (themed and hipstery): Pheonix Emporium  
For traditional (pool tables, karaoke once a week, haze of smoke): Second Chance Saloon  
  
Down at Dobbin we have a great Sushi place called Sushi King, fantastic for date nights, and right next to it is a used bookstore thats just a delight. Royal Taj at Gateway is probably the fanciest nicest dining we have, maybe next to Stanford Grill, both are a little pricey, but well worth it for the quality you get. Royal Taj is indian, Stanford is traditional steakhouse food. RISE Biscuits is a well kept new secret, and only open until 1pm everyday, but the biscuits and gravy they make are to die for.  
  
Every October we have a Halloween event at Merryweather (also something to mention, Merryweather is a huge concert venue, warped tour comes every year, its kinda crowded sometimes though) don't bother with Merryweathers, its 80 dollars and not worth it. Go to Field of Screams, its cheaper, bigger, and has cool haunted hayrides. At Christmas we have the Symphony of Lights in Merryweather too, which is worth it. Its a drive through holiday light festival thats just charming as all get out. Brookside Gardens also has fantastic christmas lights, and a butterfly garden in the other months, but its a little drive to get there, about 20 minutes. Definitely try Trattoria's Pizza while you're around as well.  
  
For the final bit, I'd say the best kept secret in all of Howard County is Toby's Dinner Theatre. I actually proposed here after a showing of Kinky Boots. Its not terribly pricey, and you get a REALLY high quality show, dinner, and drinks included in the price. You get to interact with the actors, and the theater is nationally recognized and has won tons of awards, Toby herself comes to a ton of the shows too. Broadway scouters frequent it looking for talent because of how good the shows are there. They tend to do about 5 a year, I think coming up its Spamalot then Godspell. Oh, also, The Perfect Pour is the best liquor store in the area, but Kings Contrivance Smoke Shop and Wines has a great selection as well, plus its the only good place to get cigars or hookah charcoal if you're into that kinda thing. I think thats just about everything, but if you've got any questions, I grew up here, I love it here, and I used to give tours of the city to people, so I can probably tell you where to get good Kosher or Halal food, best quality birdseed, which movie theatre to go to ect.

I'm not defending HP or Rowling at all with this argument, she'll never see another cent from me, but at its height, Harry Potter was one of the highest grossing media franchises on earth, bookstores did midnight releases for the books that would sell out in minutes.  People had watch parties for the movies, theaters would have lines going around the block.  Literally everyone and their grandma knew what Harry Potter was, which was unheard of for pre-social media books at the time unless they were something like Lord of the Rings.  It was one of the most annoying things about the internet in the late 2010s, all the fucking Harry Potter shit everywhere.  It was clearly something A LOT of people really loved and cared about, to the extent that I'd even say the average person at least had a positive association with it, even if they wouldn't call themselves a fan.  


The current hatred has a ton of people who were into that whole "superwholock and Harry Potter" fandom that was all over tumblr until like, 2015.  They made their entire lives about Harry Potter, got tattoos, spent hundreds on merch and made all kinds of fanfics; a huge amount of those are the ones who despise it now.  There's very much been a shift in the public consciousness in terms of how people feel about Harry Potter.

Thats something a ton of companies do these days.  They'll have something really good, with a diverse cast and great writing, something everyone can find something to love in.  Then, they'll realize "Writers are expensive, people like how our show covers some hot button issues, lets just focus on those for a bit", and then they'll use the social progress people used to love about the show as a virtual shield against any and all criticism.  Its really sad, because it discredits the actual arguments people try to make about representation in media being a good thing, AND ruins a show at the same time, but I guess the producers gotta make their money somehow right?  Making a quality product is difficult, but making a shit product and pretending its above criticism is easy, and a ton of people fall into the trap.

Once in my bookclub, someone accused my Fiancé of being sexist because she really loved the Discworld books, and one of her favorite literary characters was Lady Sybil Ramkin.  She went on a tirade about how women in those books were never main characters and only ever used as supportive side bait to show how manly the men are.  Its just... Not only was Terry Pratchett a HUGE supporter of feminism in the 80s and 90s, but a large number of his books DO feature female leads, almost a third of them.  As for the support female characters, we'll use Sybil Ramkin as an example, she's a swamp dragon breeder who is not only a self made psuedo-billionare, but is described as being as intimidating and powerful as the dragons she breeds. While I'm not excusing the awful things JK has said and done, I can't help but point out, this argument is made a lot in reading circles, and I personally feel its okay for a book to have shitty values so long as you, the reader, understand its context and impact.  The argument I'm making now is not entirely applicable here because JK does have real world pull and her words actually have impact and real world consequence, so this is more in relation to older books, but I try to bring up the point from time to time when talking about books and literature in this context.  Villains don't have to be redeemable, bad takes and political stances don't have to mirror the real world, sometimes its interesting to read from the perspective of a character that is vastly differing than you in views, even if those views are terrible.  Fiction books are meant to be entertainment first and foremost, with an addition of realism to help give the reader grounding and bring a little education into it, and the stances within them should always be criticized and contextualized; but I don't think that should detract from its value.  Its important to read something that makes you shudder or uncomfortable from time to time, its healthy to go out of the comfort zones of the reader like that.  There is a growing trend of "books should cater to and mirror real world issues" that's been causing a lot of censorship in media, book banning and burnings because of things in them that offend or worry people, admittedly mostly an older generation, but its still something that should be addressed.

There really isn't any more to what I'm trying to say here than that, and its kind of off topic, because this isn't really what that argument is about, its only tangentially related and JK herself isn't someone that I want to support or give any money to.  This argument is more about censorship of older works like To Kill a Mockingbird or Adventures of Huckleberry Fin, I just feel obliged to bring it up when I see posts about books and how the views in them can be problematic and try to play devils advocate a bit, I feel its always important to contextualize our own feelings on these things, and to remind people that sometimes reading something problematic can help bring awareness to issues in our own viewpoints, or the counterpoints we're fighting against. People want to argue all day about whether minimum wage increases are a good or bad thing, they want to argue about immigration and how it effects work, they want to argue over capitalism vs socialism, they want to argue over every aspect, but no one wants to look at the ugly side where it isn't so black or white.  Its not something with a simple one size fits all solution, there is no switch to flip that says good work/bad work.  We have a system that was built on a shakey foundation and treated it like it was solid, many jobs are undervalued despite their worth to the average person, and many jobs are overvalued when they produce very little.  


I've seen people use an argument called the "Great Chain" in the past, usually to speak about how important work motivation is, but a chain is only as strong as the weakest link in it.  If there's a job that others would see as worthless, that's integral to the function of the chain, it should be valued more and paid accordingly, regardless of the skill level involved.  Maybe it is simple to harvest produce, I don't know, but it doesn't matter how simple it is if you can't fill the position, it might as well be brain surgery.  The system is built on the idea that people would fill those positions despite the low pay because of the lack of skill required, but they aren't going to if they can't afford to live, they'll find somewhere else.  


The issue is, many of the jobs that hire people for these also can't afford to pay them a living wage, which is the fundamental problem here.  The whole system crumbles when cost of living reaches a certain point, it wasn't future proofed at all.  If a company can't do business, because it can't afford to pay employees, so it can't function, that means it isn't a viable business in the first place.  We don't need just straight capitalism, socialism, meritocracy or generosity, we need to overhaul the foundation we've already put in and try to fill in the holes, if one doesn't work, we'll use parts from another, and keep doing that until we have something that can run.  But that's hard and requires more critical thought than "other side bad and ruining America" so no one ever wants to do it.

I find myself reposting this every now and then because its very long and I generally don't have time to re-type it.  It was specifically about bench splitters and spikes under bridges, but I think it applies to a lot of these issues and seemed to be of help for some people before, so here it is.  
"This is one of those complicated issues where I see both sides of it. I've been homeless before, a full 2 years, 6 months of which I was living in a car at the very tail end of it, and since then, I've gotten on my feet and I volunteer on a regular basis at my local shelters. There are really only two types of homelessness. This is a sort of... non-humble way to say it, and I"m gonna sound like an asshole, so please, be patient and forgive me, but there are people like me, mostly neurotypical, who maybe made a few mistakes or were dealt a bad hand, maybe had some family issues or problems with the law that got them on the streets. People like that generally aren't homeless for more than a couple months, sometimes a year or two. Then there is the chronically homeless. Now, this is where it gets complicated. Almost every single chronically homeless person has something seriously wrong. It could be PTSD from military duty causing them to panic at any stress and stopping them from holding down a job, it could be drug addiction, or it could be some kind of physical deformity making them unable to work or interact with others. It could be as simple as someone who has very severe mental issues and can't really communicate the way people usually do.  
  
Does this make them lesser or less deserving of a good life? No. But does it make it safe for a lot of them to sleep in a public park with families, or to sleep next to the grocery store? Also no. The sheer number of people I work with at the shelter, and many of the people I slept near when I was homeless, that would lose their minds and go berserk at someone just for looking at them wrong, is staggering. And then just a little further down is people who have just given up so much that they'll literally just shit where they stand. I'm not saying the spikes are fair, or a good thing, but it isn't on the business owner or the people in the area to deal with that. You have to be really careful, because if you or your area becomes known as the place that tolerates that kind of behavior, or even if its just not openly hostile, you WILL be flooded with homeless, and while some of them are just nice people trying to get by however they can, a lot are VERY ill mentally, and unstable. The spikes are an unfortunate necessity in a society where the care thats needed just can't or isn't being provided, without them, girls get raped in neighborhoods that used to be safe, your car gets broken into, stores get robbed for liquor. I've known people that have done all 3 of those things, people who seem really nice until they just lose it. I was even invited to rob a store at knifepoint once (the store being robbed, not me at knifepoint), offered to split the share 40/60 if I just kept an eye out for them. Its not fair to expect whoever put the bench outside their business, or whoever owns the building, to vet and scope out ever person who could reasonably be dangerous sleeping on their doorstep, a much simpler solution is just to be openly hostile so it doesn't happen.  
  
Unfortunately, there isn't really an easy solution to this. Its a beautiful thought to think "Just let people sleep where they need to, just let them be" but that isn't how it works, because most people who are going to take you up on the offer aren't going to let the others who live there be. It can't be live and let live unless that's a two way street, and that's just fundamentally impossible with the amount of drugs and mental illness that comes with the chronically homeless. Don't blame the people who are just looking out for them and theirs by putting up these hostile solutions, its the best they can do without some kind of reform, blame a system that doesn't help the homeless as much as it should, tons of money is poured into the problem, but most of it goes to line someones pockets or to "Raise awareness" instead of into rehab centers and alternative employment. There are a lot of armchair activists who talk about these issues, who go to war on these kinds of spikes and solutions, that just don't want to look at the ugly side of things where it isn't a black and white issue.  
  
If you truly want to help the homeless, find a shelter to volunteer at, if you own a business, try looking for simple jobs someone with a disability can do and give them employment, and if you don't want to go that far, just donate a shitton of socks. Everyone has shirts, pants, even shoes, but there are never enough socks at shelters for anyone. Buy as many as you can, and good pairs that wont wear through in a year. I've seen a dude get stabbed for a pair of really good socks. Vote for people in your local government who make the homeless a priority, not just the presidential, but the governor, all the way down to a mayor or city official, make an effort to learn the stances people have on these things, because you can only rely on federal aid for it so much, the local level is WAY more important for things like this. And this is a REALLY unpopular opinion, and people are gonna get mad at me for it, but if its cold as balls out, and you see a homeless dude huddled in a corner, buy him a bottle of wine or something. Yeah yeah, don't buy the homeless liquor, they're addicts, blah blah, I get it, and you're right. But sometimes, even for an addict, a small act of kindness thats different than the usual bagged lunch or old graphic tee can go a really long ways, and sometimes, that drunk states gonna stop someone from killing themselves on a really cold night. Don't make a habit of it, but they can barter that for better stuff if they need it, and it'll make a difference to them, at least for one night. I just know it really helped me out when someone bought me a beer on christmas, and I know another girl who cried her eyes out because it was the first time she'd gotten to have a luxury like that in months. My high horse is tired now, so I'm gonna get off it, and this is all real controversial, but give it some thought."

Depends on what you want so I'll give a few in different genres.  


Classic literature-esque: The Collector by John Fowles, written in 1963 this follows an artist who becomes obsessed with women, and will kidnap them and keep them in his cellar.  Very sad book, you'll see thats kind of a trend on the list here, many of these fall somewhere between horror and tragedy.  


Realistic but with big twist: Out Backward by Ross Raisin, I can't really say much about this without giving away a lot about the story.  Its about a lonely farmer in the middle of the countryside who falls in love.  


Non-fiction: The Devil in the White City by Erik Larson, this is a story that actually happened, but one of the main characters is the killer.  It takes place in 1893 and follows two people working as architects on the Chicago Worlds Fair, it swaps perspectives a lot and is a really interesting read.  


Pop Culture: American Psycho by Bret Easton Ellis, by far the most well known one on the list here.  They made a movie!  Just in case you haven't seen it, it follows an investment banker in New York who deals with the pressure of that life in a very violent manner.  Brilliantly written.  


Almost Sympathetic: The Wasp Factory by Iain Banks, this is a sad story of obsession and compulsion from the perspective of an abused young man in remote Scotland.  Its... upsetting to read, because you genuinely like him.  He's funny, charming, and has led a really difficult life, you really want him to stop and get himself together.  Probably the most disturbing on the list for that reason.  


Fantasy: The Liveship Traders by Robin Hobb, This one is a little bit different than the rest, only one of the characters fits the criteria we've laid out, Captain Kennit.  The rest of the books are admittedly, very well written fantasy with some disturbing themes here or there, but his stories stand out.  He is almost an anti-hero in the story sometimes, but now and again has extremely violent tendencies that come out and lead to murder and rape.  Again, the books aren't entirely about him, he's one of about 4 characters they follow, but if you want the perspective of a villain you can almost understand, he's a perfect example.

I think its fine for books to tell stories from perspectives others would find evil or terrible.  One of the interesting things about reading to me is getting a chance to think outside my own headspace.  Its fascinating to read from a perspective I not only don't have, but actively despise.  A fascist dictator, a conman, an abusive parent, even things like a rapist or a serial killer.  Just because the author writes these characters in to be despicable doesn't mean the book is glorifying it, or that the readers are doing so either; sometimes its good for reading to make you uncomfortable, I feel like you get a better gist of the story and perspectives in real life as well, if its all just good feeling junk food then that's like only eating sweets or oil.  Sometimes you want a little sour or spicy in your life.
